This revision of geological nomenclature (Smith & Zeder, 2013) proposes the establishment of the 'Anthropocene epoch' as a distinct geological period, superseding the Holocene epoch (Haraway, 2016), in order to underscore the unprecedented and profound biophysical impact exerted by the Anthropos from the onset of the industrial era (Nixon, 2011). This paradigmatic shift in our understanding of the Earth's systems is a testament to the burgeoning field of environmental humanities, which seeks to elucidate the intricate relationships between human societies and the natural world (Latour, 2004). Furthermore, the Anthropocene concept has been subject to various critiques and debates, with some scholars arguing that it oversimplifies the complexities of human-environment interactions (Barnosky et al., 2011). Nevertheless, the notion of the Anthropocene has garnered significant attention and support from the scientific community, with many researchers recognizing the need for a new geological framework that acknowledges the profound impact of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems (Crutzen, 2007).
